title: Imaginary-time correlations in time-sliced stochastic series expansion
authors: Ryan Flynn, Adam Iaizzi, Sibin Yang, Ying-Jer Kao, Anders W. Sandvik
abstract: Combined with numerical analytic continuation techniques, quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods enable the extraction of real-frequency dynamical properties from imaginary-time correlation functions. However, the efficient computation of imaginary-time correlation functions by QMC simulations can (depending on the particular model used) be challenging, particularly for operators that are off-diagonal in the computational basis. In this work, we present an efficient and general algorithm within the stochastic series expansion (SSE) framework for evaluating imaginary-time correlation functions of both diagonal and off-diagonal operators. The algorithm builds on a discrete imaginary-time slicing of the SSE operator string, which provides correlation functions on a grid of well-defined imaginary-time points with no discretization error. For off-diagonal operators, we derive estimators that integrate directly into the existing SSE directed-loop or cluster updating schemes, introducing only minimal computational overhead. We benchmark the method on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (sampling with cluster updates) and XXZ spin chain (using directed-loop sampling), demonstrating excellent agreement (with only statistical errors) with exact diagonalization of small systems. We also study larger systems to demonstrate efficiency.
summary: This work introduces a novel, efficient algorithm within the Stochastic Series Expansion framework to compute imaginary-time correlation functions for both diagonal and off-diagonal operators. By implementing discrete imaginary-time slicing, the method overcomes previous computational bottlenecks associated with measuring non-local correlations in spin models like the TFIM and XXZ chain. This advancement significantly broadens the scope of quantum simulations for strongly correlated matter.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an efficient, general algorithm for calculating imaginary-time correlation functions in Quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
main_result: The authors present a method using discrete imaginary-time slicing of the SSE operator string that allows for the calculation of both diagonal and off-diagonal correlators with minimal overhead.
method: The technique involves splitting the inverse temperature $ eta$ into $m$ time slices ($\Delta	au =  eta/m$) within the Stochastic Series Expansion (SSE) framework. This slicing enables the direct estimation of correlation functions at discrete imaginary times $	au_k$.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked on spin systems, specifically the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and the XXZ Heisenberg chain. These models are used to test the algorithm's applicability across different types of operators.
key_observables: Imaginary-time correlation functions ($G(	au)$), including both diagonal and off-diagonal spectral functions, which can be analytically continued to real frequencies.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), number of time slices ($m$), system size ($L$), and the specific coupling constants defining the Hamiltonian (e.g., $\Delta$ for XXZ).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that discretizing imaginary time into $m$ slices provides a representation accurate enough to avoid significant discretization errors, while maintaining the ergodicity of existing cluster update schemes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the implementation details: one shows the directed-loop update for XXZ chains, and another demonstrates the TFIM cluster update mechanism used within the SSE framework.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the challenge of calculating off-diagonal correlators in QMC. It then introduces the core technique—time-slicing the SSE operator string—and derives estimators for both diagonal and off-diagonal operators. Finally, it validates this general algorithm on established models like TFIM and XXZ chains.
why_interesting: The ability to efficiently measure off-diagonal correlation functions in strongly correlated spin systems is crucial for understanding quantum phase transitions and excitations (like spinons) that are often masked by diagonal measurements.
